newsitem.title: USA: Attacks by hair-munching dolls alarm safety experts.
newsitem.headline: Attacks by hair-munching dolls alarm safety experts.

text.p: Federal safety officials warned consumers on Monday about some 35 incidents where battery-operated Cabbage Patch dolls reportedly chewed up little girls' hair and issued instructions on how to disable the chewing mechanism.
The Consumer Product Safety Commission said it was investigating the doll's safety, and advised that the chewing action can be stopped by pulling off its plastic backpack.
The agency did not order a recall of the Mattel Inc. doll, although some independent safety experts said the toy posed a danger to children.
"It ought to be recalled," product liability attorney Edward Swartz said. "Kids are going to experiment with that toy, and entanglement injuries are being reported."
The El Segundo, Calif.,-based Mattel has distributed 700,000 models of its "Cabbage Patch Snack Time Kid" since August, most of them at Christmas.

Emily Newton of Tavares, Fla., was the latest victim of the hair-eating dolls. Her doll was supposed to eat plastic celery sticks but instead it gnawed on an eight-inch strand of Emily's waist-length auburn hair Friday night, Emily's mother, Peggy Newton, said on Monday.
The 4-year-old's parents were able to remove the hair from the doll's mouth without injuring Emily or cutting her hair.

Other incidents have resulted in bald spots, shorn hair, scalp welts and some tears, but no serious injuries reported or lawsuits yet. Swartz said one girl caught her finger in the doll's masticating mouth.

The doll's packaging is not explicit about how to disable the doll, and Connecticut's consumer protection commissioner Mark Shiffrin called for Mattel to add an advisory label about the backpack and a warning label for parents to keep hair away from the doll's face.
"It does not tell you, clearly and conspicuously, how to turn the thing off," Shiffrin said.
Shiffrin said he conducted an experiment where he applied 14.5 pounds (6.6 kg) of pressure on hair caught in a doll's mouth and it would not disengage.
Some frantic parents have taken the doll apart, ripping off its head or unscrewing several screws to remove the batteries.
"All of our products undergo rigorous testing," Mattel spokeswoman Lisa McKendall said, adding that inserting only hair into the mouth should not have triggered the chewing mechanism.

The doll, a battery-powered version of one that was a huge hit with kids during Christmas in 1984, is designed to "eat" plastic french fries and other fake food and deposit it in the doll's backpack. Mattel has licensed the rights to the Cabbage Patch doll for the past three years.
Swartz blamed the toy industry for unneccesarily mechanizing a once-popular doll that required children to use their imaginations.

Last week, a doll belonging to Sarah Stevens, 7, of Griffith, Indiana, near Chicago chewed her hair up to the scalp and had to be taken apart. The girl said she only hugged the dull to her head when it began gobbling up her long locks.
"This is clearly an unintended consequence of a feeding doll and it is giving the media a feeding frenzy," said Heather Paul, director the National Safe Kids Campaign, a non-profit interest group.
She was glad parents were becoming aware of the potential risk, and suggested they exercise constant supervision over their children while playing with the doll.
